items.title: Section: The Noble-Cherished Precepts — Why an Arhat's Purity Is Measured by the Mind Itself, Not by What Has Been Severed

items.zh: 若即於此尸羅律儀無有缺犯，又復依止靜慮律儀，入諦現觀，得不還果，爾時一切惡戒種子皆悉永害。若依未至定證得初果，爾時一切能往惡趣惡戒種子皆悉永害。此即名為聖所愛戒。當知此名第二清淨力所引清淨律儀，即此亦名無漏律儀。此無漏律儀，若得阿羅漢果時，但由能治清淨勝故勝，不由所治斷勝故勝。
items.en:
Second, subsumed under the uncontaminated; first, presenting the noble-cherished precepts; first, distinguishing their character; first, revealing the non-returner's fruit. Whoever, without breach of ethical discipline, relies further on the restraint of meditative absorption to enter direct realisation of the noble truths and attain the fruit of non-returning, at that time has every seed of bad conduct permanently destroyed.
Second, revealing the stream-enterer's fruit. Whoever, relying on the concentration just prior to full absorption, attains the fruit of stream-entry, at that time has every seed of bad conduct capable of leading to a lower rebirth permanently destroyed. Second, concluding the name. This is called the noble-cherished precepts.
Second, revealing the uncontaminated; first, stating the name. One should know this is called the purified restraint brought about by this second purifying power, also called uncontaminated restraint.
Second, distinguishing its character. This uncontaminated restraint, upon attaining the fruit of arhatship, is supreme through the supremacy of the purified antidote itself, not through the supremacy of what has been eliminated by it.

items.title: Section: Eight Kinds Reduce to Three, and Why the Buddha Established Monastic, Lay, and One-Day Precepts for Three Kinds of People

items.zh: 如是八種總立唯三。一、受律儀，二、持律儀，三、清淨律儀。前二是受，防護、還引是持，下中上三通受、持二，靜慮、無漏是清淨攝。問：何故世尊建立苾芻、近事、近住三種律儀？答：由三因故。謂佛所化有三種類，或有能行離惡行行及離欲行；或有能行離惡行行，非離欲行；或不能行離惡行行及離欲行。
items.en:
Third, a careful analysis; first, a summary statement. These eight kinds are, in total, subsumed under only three: first, receiving restraint; second, sustaining restraint; third, purified restraint.
Second, the individual mapping. The first two are subsumed under receiving; guarding and restoring are subsumed under sustaining; the inferior, middling, and superior grades apply to both receiving and sustaining; and meditative absorption and the uncontaminated are subsumed under the purified.
Third, a comprehensive determination; first, clarifying its establishment; first, distinguishing the three kinds; first, establishing the reason; first, the question. Question: for what reason did the Blessed One establish three kinds of restraint — monastic ordination, lay precepts, and one-day precepts of close observance?
Second, the answer; first, stating the reason. Answer: for three reasons. Second, clarifying the meaning; first, stating and listing. The Buddha's own students are of three types: some are capable of abstaining both from unwholesome conduct and from sensory indulgence; some are capable of abstaining from unwholesome conduct but not from sensory indulgence; and some are incapable of abstaining from either.

items.zh: 依初所化類，建立苾芻律儀。依第二所化類，建立近事律儀。何以故？

items.title: Section: Why Householders Need a Different Precept — And the Eight Branches of a Single Day's Renunciation

items.zh: 非居家迫迮，現處塵俗，而能一向相續圓滿護眾學處。依第三所化類，建立近住律儀。何以故？由此不能究竟行俱離行，但當勸進攝受二因，勿彼自謂重擔所鎮。謂前三支修離惡行，其後四支修離欲行，離非梵行俱修二種。
items.en:
Third, the explanation. Household life is inherently crowded and pressured, immersed in the dust of ordinary experience, unable to maintain complete, uninterrupted, fully comprehensive guarding of many training precepts.
Third, the one-day precepts of close observance; first, stating it. According to the third type of student, the precepts of close observance are established. Second, the question raised. Why is this so? Third, the explanation; first, the general meaning. Since these students cannot ultimately abstain from both, one should simply encourage them to take up both causes for a time, without letting them feel crushed by too heavy a burden.
Second, mapping the individual branches. The first three branches cultivate abstinence from unwholesome conduct, the latter four cultivate abstinence from sensory indulgence, and abstaining from non-celibate conduct cultivates both at once.

items.title: Section: The Four Branches of Monastic Ordination — From the Formal Ceremony to Guarding Even the Smallest Precept

items.zh: 問：苾芻、近事、近住律儀，當知各由幾支所攝？答：苾芻律儀四支所攝。何等為四？一、受具足支，二、受隨法學處支，三、隨護他心支，四、隨護如所受學處支。若作表白第四羯磨，及略攝受隨麁學處。是名受具足支。由具此支故，名初苾芻具苾芻戒。自此以後，於毘奈耶別解脫中所有隨順苾芻尸羅，若彼所引眾多學處，於彼一切守護奉行，由此得名守護別解脫律儀者，是名受隨法學處支。
items.en:
Second, distinguishing the constituent branches; first, the question. Question: how many branches, respectively, comprise monastic, lay, and one-day restraint?
Second, the answer; first, monastic restraint; first, stating it. Answer: monastic restraint is subsumed under four branches. Second, the question raised. What are the four? Third, listing them. First, the branch of receiving full ordination; second, the branch of undertaking the further training precepts; third, the branch of guarding others' confidence; fourth, the branch of guarding what has been undertaken.
Fourth, explaining each; first, the branch of receiving full ordination. Whenever the formal proclamation and its threefold procedure are completed, together with a summary undertaking of the more evident training precepts, this is called the branch of receiving full ordination. By possessing this branch, one is first called a monastic possessing the monastic precepts.
Second, the branch of undertaking the further training precepts. From this point on, faithfully upholding every further training precept connected to monastic discipline as set out in the code of individual liberation, thereby earning the title of one who guards the precepts of individual liberation, is called the branch of undertaking the further training precepts.

items.title: Section: Guarding Others' Confidence and Fearing Even the Smallest Fault — The Final Two Branches of Monastic Life

items.zh: 由成就此二支者所有軌範具足、所行具足，是名隨護他心支。軌範具足、所行具足，如聲聞地已說。若於微細罪中深見怖畏，於所受學諸學處中能不毀犯；設犯能出，謂由深見怖畏及聰叡故；是名隨護如所受學處支。近事律儀由三支所攝。何等為三？
items.en:
Third, the branch of guarding others' confidence. Possessing, through these first two branches, complete proper deportment and complete proper conduct is called the branch of guarding others' confidence.
Fourth, the branch of guarding what has been undertaken. Seeing great dread even in the subtlest transgression, thereby never violating any training precept undertaken — and should a lapse occur, being able to confess and purify it, through this same dread combined with genuine intelligence — is called the branch of guarding what has been undertaken.
Second, lay restraint; first, stating it. Lay restraint is subsumed under three branches. Second, the question raised. What are the three?

items.title: Section: The Lay Precepts' Three Branches — Why Honesty About One's Own Faults Counts as Its Own Distinct Branch

items.zh: 一、受遠離最勝損他事支，二、違越所受重修行支，三、不越所受支。若永遠離損害他命、損壞他財、損他妻妾，是名初支。遠離妄語，是第二支。遠離諸酒眾放逸處，是第三支。
items.en:
Third, listing them. First, the branch of undertaking abstinence from the most serious ways of harming others; second, the branch of resuming practice after violating what has been undertaken; third, the branch of not overstepping what has been undertaken.
Fourth, explaining each; first, the first branch. Permanently abstaining from taking life, damaging property, and violating another's spouse is called the first branch.
Second, the second branch. Abstaining from false speech is the second branch. Third, the third branch. Abstaining from intoxicants and the occasions for heedlessness they create is the third branch.

items.zh: 略說近住律儀由五支所攝。何等為五？

items.title: Section: Five Branches for a Single Day — Why Renouncing Even One's Own Spouse Counts as Harming No One

items.zh: 一、受遠離損害他支，二、受遠離損害自他支，三、違越所受重修行支，四、不越所受正念住支，五、不壞正念支。若能遠離損害他命、損壞他財，是名初支。離非梵行，是第二支。所以者何？由離此者，不染習自妻妾故，不自損害；亦不染習他妻妾故，不損害他。遠離妄語，是第三支。
items.en:
Third, listing them. First, the branch of abstaining from harming others; second, the branch of abstaining from harming both self and others; third, the branch of resuming practice after violation; fourth, the branch of not overstepping settled mindfulness; fifth, the branch of not destroying mindfulness.
Fourth, explaining each; first, the first branch. Abstaining from taking life and damaging property is called the first branch.
Second, the second branch; first, stating it. Abstaining from non-celibate conduct is the second branch. Second, the question raised. Why is this so? Third, the explanation. By abstaining from this, one does not indulge even one's own spouse, and so does not harm oneself; nor does one indulge another's spouse, and so does not harm another.
Third, the third branch. Abstaining from false speech is the third branch.

items.title: Section: Guarding Mindfulness for a Single Day — Why Breaking Habitual Indulgence Keeps a Vow Firmly in Mind

items.zh: 除離諸酒眾放逸處，離餘三處，是第四支。何以故？由歌舞伎樂塗冠香鬘、昇高大床、非時飲食常所串習，若遠離彼，數數自憶；我今安住決定齋戒，於一切時堅守正念。
items.en: Fourth, the fourth branch; first, stating it. Apart from abstaining from intoxicants and the occasions for heedlessness, abstaining from the remaining three matters is the fourth branch. Second, the question raised. Why is this so? Third, the explanation. Since song, dance, and adornment, luxurious high seating, and eating after midday are all matters of constant habitual indulgence, abstaining from them causes one to repeatedly remember: I am now abiding in this firmly resolved observance, firmly guarding right mindfulness at all times.

blocks.text: Why are there separate precepts for monastics, for lay followers, and for those keeping a single day's observance? The answer is matched to what each kind of person can do.
At non-returning every seed of misconduct is destroyed. Master Cháng Bǎi: from the first to the third fruit, more and more seeds are cut; at arhatship the purity lies in the mind itself.

subs.head: Three kinds for three kinds of people

blocks.text: Master Cháng Bǎi: for those able to leave the ten unwholesome courses and also live celibate, the Buddha set monastic precepts; for those who can leave the ten courses but not desire, living as married couples, lay precepts; and for a third kind, who cannot finally keep both abstinences, the one-day observance. (Untranslated, 0590c16: monastic restraint for the first kind, lay restraint for the second; "why?")

The first three branches cultivate abstinence from wrongdoing, the latter four abstinence from sensory indulgence, and celibacy both at once. People of the third kind should be encouraged gently, lest they feel crushed by a heavy burden.

Receiving full ordination, the further training rules, guarding others' confidence, and guarding what has been received. Master Cháng Bǎi: one proclamation plus three motions, followed by the assembly's silence, shows there is no objection.
Complete deportment and conduct prevent others criticising monastics. One recovers from a lapse "through deep dread and intelligence".

Three branches: abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; from false speech; and from intoxicants. Master Cháng Bǎi: after a lapse, the condition for correction is not to lie. One who knows and admits a mistake will change.
On the day of the observance, even one's own spouse is set aside. Song, dance, adornment, high beds, and untimely meals are daily habits; abstaining from them keeps the observance in mind.
"Only one who admits a mistake will change." That is why honesty is a precept of its own.

quiz.q: What seeds of bad conduct are permanently destroyed on attaining non-returning, and on attaining stream-entry through the preliminary concentration?
options: stream-entry destroys every seed of bad conduct; non-returning destroys those capable of leading to a lower rebirth
non-returning destroys every seed of bad conduct; stream-entry destroys those capable of leading to a lower rebirth
both only suppress them; destruction comes only with arhatship
both destroy every seed, and so both are called beyond training
quiz.why: The treatise says that on attaining the fruit of non-returning every seed of bad conduct is permanently destroyed, while stream-entry through the concentration prior to full absorption destroys every such seed capable of leading to a lower rebirth. Master Cháng Bǎi: the seeds leading to the three evil destinies are destroyed forever. This is what is called the noble-cherished precepts.

quiz.q: Why is uncontaminated restraint at arhatship supreme through the purified antidote, not through what is eliminated?
options: an arhat's seeds of bad conduct are not all severed, so supremacy cannot rest on what is cut
stream-entry already cuts all such seeds, so the four fruits are equal in what is cut
up to non-returning more is cut as one goes; by arhatship the seeds are already gone, and the supremacy lies in the fully pure antidote
antidote and what it treats are both provisional, so the supremacy is only a manner of speaking
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the pure restraint of noble ones from the first through the third fruit is excellent because more and more seeds of bad conduct are severed. At arhatship the point changes: the mind that is the antidote is wholly pure, and the supremacy is not spoken of in terms of the seeds severed, since every seed of bad conduct had already been destroyed at non-returning.

quiz.q: How are the eight restraints mapped onto the three?
options: the first two are sustaining; guarding and restoring are receiving; the three grades both; absorption and the uncontaminated purified
the first four are receiving; the three grades sustaining; absorption and the uncontaminated purified
the first two are receiving; guarding and restoring sustaining; the three grades both; absorption and the uncontaminated purified
the first two are receiving; the other six sustaining; the purified lies outside the eight
quiz.why: The treatise maps the first two, arousing and receiving, to receiving; guarding and restoring to sustaining; the inferior, middling, and superior grades to both; and meditative absorption and the uncontaminated to the purified. Master Cháng Bǎi: receiving the precepts has lower, middle, and upper grades, and so does keeping them, which is why the three grades apply to both.

quiz.q: Why did the Blessed One establish three restraints? How does Master Cháng Bǎi match them to the three types of student?
options: those able to leave both take the eight precepts; those leaving evil but not desire take monastic precepts; those unable to do so for life take lay precepts
those able to leave both take monastic precepts; those leaving evil but not desire lay precepts; those unable to do so for life the eight-precept observance
by age: the young take the one-day precepts, the middle-aged lay precepts, and the old monastic ones
by capacity: the dull take monastic precepts, the middling one-day precepts, and the sharp lay precepts
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: for those able to leave the evil conduct of the ten courses and also practice celibacy, the Buddha established monastic precepts; the second type can leave the ten courses but not desire, and still live as married couples; for those unable to leave both for life he established the eight-precept observance. So the three restraints answer to what each type of person can actually do.

quiz.q: 離欲行 is rendered with "sexual activity" in §18 and "sensory indulgence" in §19. Going by the lecture, what is its range?
options: only sexual desire; §19's "sensory indulgence" is too wide and should be changed throughout
only abstaining from intoxicants; both renderings are wrong and it should be so translated
abstaining from enjoying form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and sexual desire; §18's "sexual activity" is narrower, and one term has two renderings
abstaining from the ten courses of action; both renderings are wrong and it should read "unwholesome conduct," the same as the first three branches
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: abstaining from enjoying form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and sexual desire is called the practice of leaving desire. The narrower "sexual activity" of §18 would not fit the latter branches of the one-day precepts, such as adornment, high beds, and untimely meals, so §19's "sensory indulgence" suits better, and one Chinese term ought not to have two renderings.

quiz.q: How does the treatise assign the branches of the one-day precepts to the two practices?
options: the first three cultivate leaving evil conduct, the latter four leaving desire, and celibacy both
the first four cultivate leaving evil conduct, the latter three leaving desire, and celibacy only the latter
all eight cultivate leaving evil conduct, and leaving desire comes with monastic precepts
all eight cultivate leaving desire, and leaving evil conduct comes with the five precepts
quiz.why: The treatise says the first three branches cultivate abstinence from unwholesome conduct, the latter four abstinence from sensory indulgence, and abstaining from non-celibate conduct cultivates both at once. Master Cháng Bǎi: not engaging in sexual conduct is both leaving evil conduct and leaving desire, since it concerns both harming another and one's own indulgence.

quiz.q: Which four branches comprise monastic restraint?
options: receiving full ordination, undertaking further training precepts, guarding others' confidence, guarding what has been undertaken
abstaining from harming others, resuming practice after violation, not overstepping what was undertaken, not destroying mindfulness
arousing restraint, receiving restraint, guarding restraint, and restoring restraint
restraint of precepts, of absorption, the uncontaminated, and the inferior
quiz.why: The treatise lists the branches of receiving full ordination, undertaking the further training precepts, guarding others' confidence, and guarding what has been undertaken. Master Cháng Bǎi: receiving full ordination is the first condition of being a monk. The second option mixes branch names of the lay and one-day precepts, and the third lists four of the eight restraints.

quiz.q: The English has "the formal proclamation and its threefold procedure" for 表白第四羯磨. Why does the Chinese say "fourth" and the English "threefold"?
options: one proclamation and three motions make four; the Chinese names the fourth that completes it, the English the three motions, and both mean the same
the Chinese has four motions and the English omits one, so it should be "fourfold procedure"
the Chinese refers to the nuns' rite and the English to the monks', and these differ
fourth means a monk's fourth year after ordination, nothing to do with the number of motions
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: when the one proclamation and three motions are done, the silence of the assembly shows there is no objection. One proclamation plus three motions makes four announcements, so the Chinese names the fourth, which completes the act, while the English counts the three motions. Neither is wrong, but a reader comparing them should know both describe one rite.

quiz.q: What is the branch of undertaking the further training precepts?
options: the proclamation and motions at ordination, with a summary undertaking of evident rules
seeing dread even in subtle faults, and clearing any lapse
after ordination, guarding and upholding all the training that accords with monastic discipline in the code and what it entails
complete deportment and conduct, giving others no cause for criticism
quiz.why: The treatise says that from ordination on, one guards and upholds all that accords with monastic discipline in the code of individual liberation, and the many training rules it entails. Master Cháng Bǎi: all that accords with the monastic precepts, and the many related matters to be learned, must be guarded and upheld. The other options describe the first, fourth, and third branches.

quiz.q: Why is the third branch said to guard others' minds, according to Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: by cultivating knowledge of others' minds, one sees what others think
by constantly urging others to take precepts, one rouses their good minds and their rejoicing
by making deportment and conduct complete, one prevents others from criticising monastics
by not speaking of others' faults, one keeps them from anger
quiz.why: The treatise defines this branch as complete deportment and complete conduct by one who possesses the first two branches. Master Cháng Bǎi: doing these well prevents others from criticising monastics, and this is the branch of guarding others' minds. So what is guarded is others' confidence, as the English "guarding others' confidence" rightly conveys.

quiz.q: On what does "should a lapse occur, being able to confess and purify it" depend?
options: on deep dread together with intelligence
on the assembly's accusation and a teacher's care
on donors' offerings and on being praised
on suppression by absorption and destruction by the path
quiz.why: The treatise says one can emerge from a lapse through deep dread and intelligence. Master Cháng Bǎi: a monk who sees great fault in subtle transgressions feels deep fear, and through intelligence, after a momentary lapse, at once applies the remedy and repents to purity. The English keeps this: "through this same dread combined with genuine intelligence."

quiz.q: How do the three branches of lay restraint correspond to the five precepts?
options: the first is killing and stealing; the second sexual misconduct and false speech; the third intoxicants
the first is false speech; the second killing, stealing, and misconduct; the third intoxicants
the first is killing; the second stealing and misconduct; the third false speech and intoxicants
the first is killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the second false speech; the third intoxicants
quiz.why: The treatise's first branch covers abstaining from taking life, damaging property, and violating another's spouse; the second is abstaining from false speech; the third from intoxicants and the occasions for heedlessness. Master Cháng Bǎi: the branch of abstaining from the gravest harm to others is not killing, not stealing, and no sexual misconduct.

quiz.q: Why is abstaining from false speech the branch of resuming practice after violation?
options: to reform after a lapse one must not lie; one who lies and will not admit fault will not change
false speech is the gravest of the five, so a lapse in it requires receiving the precepts over again
false speech breaks harmony, so the community must rule on it anew
false speech counts only when violating the other four, not otherwise
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: after a lapse one must reform, and the condition for correction is not to lie; a person who lies and will not admit fault will not change, and only one who knows and admits a mistake will change. So honesty about one's own fault is what makes resuming practice possible, which is why this precept has that name.

quiz.q: Among the five branches of the one-day precepts, why is abstaining from non-celibate conduct the branch of not harming self and others?
options: not indulging another's spouse one does not harm oneself; not indulging one's own spouse one does not harm another
keeping this branch spares one's parents and family all suffering
keeping this branch also fulfils not killing and not stealing
not indulging one's own spouse one does not harm oneself; not indulging another's one does not harm another
quiz.why: The treatise explains that one does not indulge one's own spouse and so does not harm oneself, and does not indulge another's spouse and so does not harm another. Master Cháng Bǎi: not only sexual misconduct but also marital relations are given up here; not indulging one's own spouse is the practice of leaving desire that does not harm oneself.

quiz.q: Why does giving up song and dance, high beds, and untimely meals support right mindfulness?
options: these three are grave root offenses in themselves, and abstaining removes karmic obstruction and evil rebirth
abstaining makes the body light, so that one can sit in absorption
these are daily habits of laypeople; abstaining keeps reminding one that one has taken the eight precepts
the Buddha taught only on observance days, and clarity helps one remember
quiz.why: Song, dance, adornment, high beds, and untimely meals are matters of constant habit, so abstaining from them makes one repeatedly recall the observance. Master Cháng Bǎi: for lay followers these are habitual matters of daily life; abstaining from them means constantly reminding oneself that one has taken the eight precepts. The break in habit itself serves as the reminder.
